143: 
144: ## Part 5: Technical Architecture
145: 
146: ### Data Flow
147: 
148: ```
149: Checkpoint Created
150:     ↓
151: Prompts Extracted from Transcript
152:     ↓
153: Stored in Git Branch
154:     ├── Prompt text (full)
155:     ├── Embedding vector (future)
156:     └── Metadata (checkpoint_id, session_id, timestamp)
157:     ↓
158: User Queries
159:     ↓
160: Local Index (SQLite) ← New component
161:     ↓
162: Results Displayed
163: ```
164: 
165: ### Components to Build
166: 
167: ```
168: cmd/entire/cli/prompts/
169: ├── prompts.go           # Main command group
170: ├── list.go             # entire prompts list
171: ├── search.go           # entire prompts search  
172: ├── show.go             # entire prompts show
173: ├── diff.go             # entire prompts diff (prompt + files)
174: ├── indexer.go          # Build/update local prompt index
175: ├── store.go            # SQLite-based prompt storage
176: ├── embed.go            # (Future) Embedding generation
177: └── test/
178:     ├── prompts_test.go
179:     ├── search_test.go
180:     └── indexer_test.go
181: ```
182: 
183: ### Data Model
184: 
185: ```go
186: // Local prompt store
187: type PromptStore struct {
188:     db *sql.DB
189: }
190: 
191: type Prompt struct {
192:     ID            string    // UUID
193:     CheckpointID  string    // From checkpoint
194:     SessionID     string    // From session
195:     Text          string    // Full prompt text
196:     Timestamp     time.Time
197:     Agent         string    // "Claude Code", etc.
198:     Model         string    // "claude-opus-4"
199:     FilesChanged  []string // Files in this checkpoint
200:     Branch        string
201:     Author        string    // Git author
202: }
203: 
204: type SearchResult struct {
205:     Prompt   Prompt
206:     Score    float64      // Similarity score
207:     Matches  []string     // Matching terms
208:     Context  string       // Surrounding context (files)
209: }
210: ```
211: 
212: ### Index Strategy
213: 
214: **Phase 1: Full-text search (immediate)**
215: ```sql
216: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE prompts USING fts5(
217:     text,
218:     checkpoint_id UNINDEXED,
219:     session_id UNINDEXED
220: );
221: ```
222: 
223: **Phase 2: Semantic search (future)**
224: - Generate embeddings from prompts
225: - Store vectors alongside text
226: - Use cosine similarity for ranking
227: - Can use local model (llama.cpp) or API
228: 
229: **Phase 3: Cross-repo search (future)**
230: - Push index to checkpoint remote
231: - Search across team's history
232: - Privacy controls
233: 
234: ---
235: 
236: ## Part 6: Algorithms & Methods
237: 
238: ### Search Algorithm Comparison
239: 
240: | Algorithm | Pros | Cons | Recommendation |
241: |-----------|------|------|----------------|
242: | **BM25** | Fast, good for keyword | No semantic understanding | Phase 1 fallback |
243: | **TF-IDF** | Simple, interpretable | Ignores word order | Not recommended |
244: | **Dense Retrieval** | Semantic matching | Needs embeddings | Phase 2 |
245: | **Hybrid (BM25 + Dense)** | Best of both | Complexity | Phase 2+ |
246: 
247: ### Recommended Approach: TF-IDF + Trigram (Phase 1)
248: 
249: ```go
250: // Simple but effective for local prompts
251: // Based on PostgreSQL's pg_trgm + ts_rank pattern
252: 
253: type PromptSearcher struct {
254:     db *sql.DB
255: }
256: 
257: func (s *PromptSearcher) Search(query string, limit int) ([]Prompt, error) {
258:     // 1. Tokenize query
259:     tokens := tokenize(query)
260:     
261:     // 2. Build weighted SQL query
262:     // - Exact phrase matches: high weight
263:     // - Individual word matches: medium weight
264:     // - All tokens must match (AND semantics)
265:     
266:     sql := `
267:         SELECT p.*, 
268:             ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', p.text), query) as rank
269:         FROM prompts p, to_tsquery('english', ?) as query
270:         WHERE to_tsvector('english', p.text) @@ query
271:         ORDER BY rank DESC
272:         LIMIT ?
273:     `
274:     
275:     return s.db.Query(sql, tokens, limit)
276: }
277: ```
278: 
279: ### Semantic Search (Phase 2)
280: 
281: **Option 1: Local embeddings (Privacy-first)**
282: ```bash
283: # Embedding model (quantized, ~1GB)
284: sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2
285: ```
286: 
287: **Option 2: API-based (Simpler)**
288: ```bash
289: # Use existing provider
290: openai embeddings / anthropic embeddings
291: ```
292: 
293: **Hybrid Ranking Formula:**
294: ```
295: FinalScore = α × BM25Score + (1-α) × CosineSimilarity
296: ```
297: - α = 0.3 for prompts (semantic > keyword)
298: 
299: ---
300: 
301: ## Part 7: Edge Cases
302: 
303: ### 1. Large Transcripts
304: - **Problem:** Single session can have 100+ prompts
305: - **Solution:** Index all prompts; show session grouping in results
306: 
307: ### 2. Multi-turn Context
308: - **Problem:** "Continue" or follow-up prompts lack full context
309: - **Solution:** Include parent prompt reference; show conversation thread
310: 
311: ### 3. Binary/File Prompts
312: - **Problem:** Some prompts are just "fix tests" with no detail
313: - **Solution:** Use checkpoint description as fallback; warn on weak prompts
314: 
315: ### 4. Non-English Prompts
316: - **Problem:** Tokenizers/embeddings may not handle mixed languages
317: - **Solution:** UTF-8 support; language detection; separate indexes
318: 
319: ### 5. Privacy/Sensitive Prompts
320: - **Problem:** Prompts may contain secrets, PII
321: - **Solution:** Re-use existing PII redaction; exclude from index option
322: 
323: ### 6. Offline Mode
324: - **Problem:** User disconnected from internet
325: - **Solution:** Local SQLite index works offline; cross-repo needs connectivity
326: 
327: ### 7. Fresh Index
328: - **Problem:** No prompts indexed yet

---
title: "The Entire CLI: How It Works & Where It's Headed"
description: AI generated PRs are creating a massive code review bottleneck. Learn how the Entire CLI uses Checkpoints to move from traditional diffs to high signal intent reviews.
category: Engineering
author: Rizèl Scarlett
---

"I don't even read the code my agents produce" is the ultimate developer flex of 2026.

But it is really a coping mechanism. There is simply too much code to review. Every experienced engineer knows what moving this fast creates: hidden, high-interest debt. That's fine for a weekend, vibe-coded project. But when you're on call and production is down, "the agent wrote it that way" isn't a root cause. Without a time machine, you're debugging a black box.

In traditional engineering, git commits served us well. They show us _what_ changed. But both at the speed of AI and for team coherence, that's no longer enough. We need to understand the _why_.

What prompt was given? What was the chain of agents and subagents that produced this? What alternatives were tried and discarded? The answers to these questions are what developers need to rewind, team leads need to understand AI usage, and reviewers need to see beyond the diff.

Checkpoints are our initial answer.

A richer primitive than commits, capturing not just what changed, but the context behind it.

## What's a Checkpoint?

A [Checkpoint](https://docs.entire.io/cli/checkpoints) is a single, addressable unit that bundles everything behind a change: the code state, the agent's full transcript, your prompts, token usage, and line-level attribution showing how much the agent wrote versus what you edited. Each Checkpoint gets a 12-character ID, stored in git and included in your commit via a trailer, so you can trace any change back to the exact session that produced it.

![Anatomy of a Checkpoint](/blog/the-entire-cli-how-it-works-and-where-its-headed/anatomy_of_a_checkpoint_v3.svg)

When Checkpoints are pushed to a shared remote, anyone can see how AI and a human built a feature together, not just what changed.

## How it works

Developers are already accustomed to working with an agent and committing code, and we didn't want to disrupt that existing developer experience. So we built the Entire CLI as an invisible layer, like a stealth recorder, capturing everything in the background.

That led to one strict constraint: everything had to fit inside a normal git workflow, from capturing sessions to storing metadata and linking it to commits. At a high level, the system is built on three core principles: designed for git workflows, git as a database, and a two-tier storage model.

### Designed for Git Workflows

Entire fits into your existing git workflow without changing how you work.

Because the Checkpoint ID is stored in a commit trailer and not tied to a commit hash, it survives commonly used git operations that rewrite commit history, like rebase, amend, squash, and cherry-pick. Instead of breaking when commits are rewritten, the link between your code and its session history remains intact.

That same separation extends to how the data is stored. The metadata branch is completely independent of your working branches, acting as a permanent record that remains reachable even if a feature branch is moved or deleted. Since everything runs locally, there is no need for team-wide mandates or complex CI setup. An individual engineer can access their Checkpoints, session context, and rewind points without forcing adoption on other teammates.

### Git as a Database

Everything Entire records, transcripts, prompts, attribution, summaries, is stored as git objects. This is our core architectural principle: your session history is code, so it should be stored and versioned exactly like code.

Depending on your team's workflow, you can choose where those objects live:

**Same repository**
By default, Checkpoint metadata lives on a separate branch called entire/checkpoints/v1 that travels with your repository. When you push your code, your session history goes with it. When someone clones the repo, they get the full context too.

**Decoupled repository**
For teams that need more control, Checkpoints can be stored in a separate repository. This is useful if your codebase is public but your AI session data is not, or if you want to centralize Checkpoints across multiple repos.

This approach is valuable for a few reasons:

- It builds on existing git infrastructure instead of introducing a new database, SaaS product, or proprietary storage layer.
- Because session history lives in git, it moves with the workflow across different hosts, during offline work, or when switching remotes.
- Every change to session history is tracked, providing the same auditability and rollback capabilities expected from git.

### Two-tier Storage Model

We use a two-tier storage model for temporary and permanent Checkpoints.

You need the ability to rewind mid-session if an agent goes sideways, so we provide Checkpoints before you commit. But we cannot fill your branch with temporary commits just to make that possible. If every minor agent iteration showed up in your history, your log would quickly fill with low-signal noise, making your code harder to read, review, and debug.

To avoid that, the Entire CLI writes those Checkpoints to shadow branches. Shadow branches are temporary, out-of-band branches that store Checkpoint data while you work. They follow a specific naming convention: `entire/<commit-hash-7-chars>-<worktree-hash-6-chars>`, and stay completely separate from your working branch. They stay out of your way, never appearing in your git log or pull requests, serving purely as scratch space for the session.

![Pre-commit state showing shadow branches](/blog/the-entire-cli-how-it-works-and-where-its-headed/pre_commit_state_animated.gif)

Once you commit, that temporary state is condensed into a permanent record, with transcripts, prompts, file changes, token usage, and attribution written to a dedicated Checkpoints branch and linked to your commit via a trailer.

![Post-commit state showing permanent checkpoints](/blog/the-entire-cli-how-it-works-and-where-its-headed/post_commit_state_animated.gif)

While the principles stayed the same, the implementation had to evolve.

## What's Changed Since Launch

When we launched Entire, we had a simple mental model: a hook fires, data is captured, the user commits, done. That worked for single-agent, single-session workflows.

Real-world engineering isn't linear. You rebase mid-session, you stash changes, and you often run multiple agents at once. To handle this, we moved away from simple hooks and formalized how sessions behave. Sessions are now treated as a state machine with explicit phases (IDLE, ACTIVE, ENDED) managed in `.git/entire-sessions/`.

This architectural shift unlocked the following features:

- **Concurrent sessions:** You can run two agents in the same repository at the same time. For example, a Claude Code session in one terminal and Cursor in another, each tracked independently.
- **Interrupted workflows:** You can rebase or stash mid-session without losing Checkpoints.
- **Line-level attribution:** Every Checkpoint tracks which lines of code came from the agent versus which came from you.
- **Subagent tracking:** When an agent spawns a subagent, it receives its own nested Checkpoint. This preserves the full chain of command so you can see exactly how a high-level goal was decomposed into smaller agentic actions.
- **Multi-agent support:** Entire is agent-agnostic, supporting Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Factory AI Droid, OpenCode, and external agent protocols.
- **Separate checkpoint repository:** You now have the choice to store Checkpoint data in a separate repository from your main code. This is useful when your codebase is public but your AI session data is not, or when teams want to centralize checkpoint data across multiple repos.

## Where We're Headed

Now that we've turned raw developer activity into structured, reliable data, the Checkpoint becomes a new semantic unit, richer than commits, queryable, and shareable.

From here, we start to build toward team visibility, search, auditability, and a different way to think about code review.

### Team Visibility

Git tells you who committed the code. Entire shows how it was built, recording token usage, agent type, and attribution directly in the repository so the invisible parts of development become a shared signal.

When a feature ships with 90% agent-generated code, that context will help the whole team. The author gets better feedback, reviewers know where to focus, and the next person to touch that code knows what they're walking into.

### Search

Traditional `git log` answers "what changed," but in today's workflows a more pressing question is "why did we do it this way?"

We're making that answer searchable. Users will be able to surface the prompt that introduced a workaround or revisit the reasoning behind a library choice months later. The "why" will be part of your history.

### Audit and Transparency

In regulated industries like finance, healthcare, and defense, "who wrote this code" has direct implications for compliance, liability, and safety. The Entire CLI will solve this by capturing accurate attribution and authorship at commit time. By mapping every step from human prompt to agent response to final human refinement, it makes clear what part the human played versus the agent.

### Rethinking Code Review to Intent Review

Code review was built for a human pace. But with agents shipping entire features in a single session, reviewers are drowning in massive diffs and defaulting to approving with a measly "LGTM." The issue is already so prevalent that some open source maintainers are banning agent-authored contributions.

Checkpoints are the foundation, but the next step is a shift in methodology. We are moving beyond the diff to replace code reviews with intent reviews. This positions reviewers to start with intent by examining the prompt, the session transcript, and the reasoning behind key decisions. Instead of parsing 500 lines of syntax, they focus on the problem being solved and whether the right calls were made along the way.

---

At Entire, we're actively building the world's next developer platform in the open. If you're experimenting with agents, join the [Discord](https://discord.gg/hsV7HTsk5p), share what you're seeing, and help shape where this goes next.

- [Read the docs](https://docs.entire.io/introduction)
- [Join the Discord](https://discord.gg/hsV7HTsk5p)
- [Follow our progress on GitHub](https://github.com/entireio)

we launched Entire
[...]
mental model: a hook fires, data is captured, the user commits, done. That worked for single-agent, single-session workflows.
[...]
Real-world engineering isn't linear. You rebase mid-session, you stash changes, and you often run multiple agents at once. To handle this, we moved away from simple hooks and formalized how sessions behave. Sessions are now treated as a state machine with explicit phases (IDLE, ACTIVE, ENDED) managed in `.git/entire-sessions/`.
[...]
- Concurrent sessions: You can run two agents
[...]
same time. For example, a Claude Code session in one terminal and Cursor in another, each tracked
[...]

[...]
- Multi-agent support: Entire is agent-agnostic, supporting Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Factory AI Droid, OpenCode, and external agent protocols.
[...]
- Separate checkpoint repository: You now have the choice to store Checkpoint data in a separate repository from your main code. This is useful when your codebase is public but your AI session data is not, or when teams want to centralize checkpoint data across multiple repos.
[...]
## Where We're Headed
[...]
Now that we've turned raw developer activity into structured, reliable data, the Checkpoint becomes a new semantic unit, richer than commits, queryable, and shareable.
[...]
From here, we start to build toward team visibility, search, auditability, and a different way to think about code review.
[...]
Git tells you who committed the code. Entire shows how it was built, recording token usage, agent type, and attribution directly in the repository so the invisible parts of development become a shared signal.
[...]

The Entire CLI will solve this by capturing accurate attribution and authorship at commit time. Instead of parsing 500 lines of syntax, they focus on the problem being solved and whether the right calls were made along the way.

Highlights:
You can now bring your own agent to the Entire CLI. Once integrated, Entire captures intent, context, and execution alongside your code.
[...]
Since launching in February, we've added native support for popular agents including Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor, FactoryAI, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot CLI. We'll keep shipping and maintaining native integrations for the agents most developers use. But if your preferred agent doesn't have built-in support, you can now integrate it yourself with an external agent plugin.
[...]
You don't need to edit Entire's source code to add support for a new agent. Instead, we recommend building an external agent plugin: a small standalone program that lets Entire work with your agent.
[...]
There are two ways to build an external agent plugin. You can use the External Agents Skill, or you can build one from scratch. Our External Agent Plugin docs cover the full architecture in detail.
[...]
The fastest way to build a plugin is with the workflow we've set up in the external-agents repo. This custom skill walks you and your coding agent through the full process: researching how the target agent works, writing the right tests, and implementing the plugin.
[...]
We also provide a companion test suite, so you can verify that your plugin follows the rules for communicating with Entire. If you want a starting point for your own plugin, we built `roger-roger` as a reference implementation you can adapt to your agent.
[...]
If you prefer, you can also build the plugin from scratch. Let's walk through what that looks like in practice. We'll use Pi, one of our most recent integrations, as a concrete example.
[...]
For Entire to communicate with your plugin, it expects a set of subcommands that let it gather information and trigger actions. You must implement a core
[...]
set, including `info`, `detect`, `install-hooks`, `parse-hook`, and `read-transcript
[...]
Agent hooks are how the Entire CLI observes what an agent is doing. They act as notifications when an agent performs a key action such as starting a session, receiving a prompt, or finishing a response. Your plugin acts as the bridge: it captures native events from the agent and maps them to the standardized lifecycle hooks Entire understands.
[...]
Entire captures Checkpoints, which are snapshots of both code changes and the session context behind them. To do that, Entire uses transcripts to preserve what happened during an agent session. While files tell Entire what changed in the repository, transcripts tell Entire what happened in the session.
[...]
Your plugin needs to tell Entire where the transcript lives so it can read it. For Pi, transcripts are stored as `JSONL` session files. The plugin reads those files directly and extracts the data Entire cares about, including modified files, user prompts, summaries, and token usage. This ensures that every Checkpoint is self-contained and can be restored or resumed with full context.
[...]
Entire will discover the plugin, run its installation hooks, and start tracking your sessions. To verify everything is working, run a real session with your agent. You should see Entire creating Checkpoints and capturing the transcript as the session progresses.
[...]
Bringing your own agent to Entire means you don't have to wait for first-party support before your workflow can benefit from Checkpoints, transcripts, and session context.
[...]
If an agent you rely on isn't supported yet, you can integrate it yourself and keep your existing workflow while gaining a full development history alongside your code.

# Entire CLI: Version Control for Your Agent Sessions
[...]
When you use AI coding agents like Claude Code, the code stays but the conversation disappears. You get the commit, but not why the agent made the choices it did. Entire fixes that.
[...]
It hooks into your git workflow to capture AI sessions — prompts, responses, files touched, token usage — and stores them on a separate git branch (`entire/checkpoints/v1`). Your commit history stays clean. The context lives alongside it.

## 30s Setup
[...]
That's it. Work with Claude Code or Gemini CLI normally. When you push, Entire prompts you to link the commit to your session. If you say yes, the session gets pushed to your repo as a checkpoint.
[...]
Entire has two strategies:`manual-commit`(default) and`auto-commit`. I'd recommend auto-commit — it creates a checkpoint after every agent response, so you get fine-grained save points without having to remember to commit yourself:
[...]
## Rewind
[...]
The standout feature. Entire saves checkpoints as you go. If things go sideways, roll back:
[...]
Pick a checkpoint, code snaps back. No`git stash`, no manual undo. You can also use`entire explain` to review what happened in a session or`entire resume` to pick up where you left off.
[...]
## Real Example
[...]
I used Claude Code to refactor the navigation on this blog — making the header consistent across all pages. Entire captured the full session automatically.
[...]
Running`entire explain` shows each checkpoint with the original prompt and resulting commit. And`entire rewind` gives you an interactive picker to roll back to any save point:
[...]
## Works Across Machines
[...]
The config files (`.entire/settings.json`,`.claude/settings.json`) get committed to your repo. On a new machine, just install the CLI and re-enable hooks:
[...]
Sessions from all your machines push to the same checkpoint branch.
[...]
## What It Doesn't Touch
[...]
Entire is local dev tooling. No build changes, no CI/CD impact, no new dependencies. Your deploys stay exactly the same.
[...]
## One More Thing
[...]
Honestly, this feels like something that should just be built into Claude Code. Running a separate CLI for session history adds friction. But the tradeoff makes sense — Entire is agent-agnostic (works with Gemini CLI too) and stores everything in git, not a vendor's cloud. If Anthropic built it in natively, it'd only cover Claude. Having it as a git layer means the history lives in your repo regardless of which agent wrote the code.
[...]
Overall it was a good experience getting it set up across my projects. I'm excited to see how it evolves.
[...]
Check it out: entire.io· GitHub· Docs

Entire will be based on three key components: a git-compatible database that unifies code, intent, constraints, and reasoning in a single version-controlled system; a universal semantic reasoning layer that enables multi-agent coordination through the context graph; and an AI-native software development lifecycle to reinvent agent-to-human collaboration.

[...]
## Our first release: The Entire CLI to track agent context
[...]
Checkpoints are a new primitive that automatically captures agent context as first-class, versioned data in Git. When you commit code generated by an agent, Checkpoints capture the full session alongside the commit: the transcript, prompts, files touched, token usage, tool calls and more. This context becomes the foundational write-path of our semantic reasoning layer. You can browse checkpoints by branch, drill into individual sessions, and trace how your codebase evolved through human-and-agent collaboration commit by commit.
[...]
Our plan is to support Checkpoints for every agent. Today, Entire CLI ships with support for Anthropic's Claude Code and Google Gemini CLI. Codex, Cursor CLI, and other agents coming soon.
[...]
Checkpoints run as a Git-aware CLI. On every commit generated by an agent, it writes a structured checkpoint object and associates it with the commit SHA. The code stays exactly the same, we just add context as first-class metadata. When you push your commit, Checkpoints also pushes this metadata to a separate branch (entire/checkpoints/v1), giving you a complete, append-only audit log inside your repository. As a result, every change can now be traced back not only to a diff, but to the reasoning that produced it.
[...]

[...]

[...]
Checkpoints are our first step towards building a universal semantic reasoning layer for agents. Today, it gives you traceability and history. Tomorrow, it will become the shared memory that allows agents to coordinate, hand off context and build together without collision or loss of understanding.
[...]
Most importantly, we're releasing the Entire CLI open source project because we believe that this layer should be portable, independent, and available for every single agent or model. And because we know, we are better with the contributions of the interconnected community of open-source developers.

240: | Algorithm | Pros | Cons | Recommendation |

257: func (s *PromptSearcher) Search(query string, limit int) ([]Prompt, error) {

262:     // - Exact phrase matches: high weight
263:     // - Individual word matches: medium weight
264:     // - All tokens must match (AND semantics)

266:     sql := `

268:             ts_rank(to_tsvector('english', p.text), query) as rank
269:         FROM prompts p, to_tsquery('english', ?) as query
270:         WHERE to_tsvector('english', p.text) @@ query
271:         ORDER BY rank DESC
272:         LIMIT ?
273:     `

# Feature Proposal: Searchable Prompts CLI

**Feature:** `entire prompts search` — Searchable prompts from checkpoint history
**Roadmap:** https://entire.io/blog/the-entire-cli-how-it-works-and-where-its-headed (March 2026)
**Status:** Not shipped, not in progress
**Updated:** May 2026

---

## 1. Problem Statement

> "We're making that answer searchable. Users will be able to surface the prompt that introduced a workaround or revisit the reasoning behind a library choice months later. The 'why' will be part of your history." — Entire Roadmap

Developers can search **what changed** (git blame, grep) but cannot search **why it changed** — the prompts that led to decisions.

**Example:** "Why did we pick Redis over Memcached?"
- Grep for "redis" → finds usage, not decision
- Git blame → shows who, not why
- Slack/Notion/Google Docs → fragmented
- Ask teammates → unreliable

**With searchable prompts:**
```
$ entire prompts search "cache decision"
→ "Why did we choose Redis over Memcached?"  a3b2c4d5e6f7  2026-03-15  Claude Code
→ "Add Redis caching for session store"       7f8e9d1a2b3c  2026-04-02  Gemini CLI
```

---

## 2. Roadmap Alignment

| Feature | Status | Roadmap Section |
|---------|--------|----------------|
| **Searchable Prompts** | NOT SHIPPED | "Search" — surfacing the prompt that introduced a workaround |
| Intent Review | NOT SHIPPED | "Rethinking Code Review to Intent Review" |
| Team Visibility | NOT SHIPPED | "Team Visibility" |
| Audit & Transparency | Partial | Line-level attribution exists |

**This proposal covers only "Searchable Prompts."** Intent review is a separate feature.

---

## 3. Current Architecture

### What Already Exists

```
Checkpoint Condensation
      ↓
GitStore.WriteCommitted()
      ↓
entire/checkpoints/v1 branch
      ↓
<checkpoint-id[:2]>/<checkpoint-id[2:]>/
├── metadata.json           # CheckpointSummary (no prompts)
├── 0/                       # Session 0
│   ├── metadata.json        # CommittedMetadata
│   ├── full.jsonl          # Transcript
│   └── prompt.txt           # User prompts (multi-turn, split by "---\n\n")
├── 1/                       # Session 1 (if multi-session)
...
```

**Key types (from `checkpoint/checkpoint.go`):**
```go
type CheckpointSummary struct {
    CheckpointID     id.CheckpointID
    Sessions         []SessionFilePaths  // paths to session dirs
    FilesTouched     []string
    HasReview        bool
}

type CommittedMetadata struct {
    SessionID        string
    Agent            types.AgentType
    Model            string
    CreatedAt        time.Time
    CheckpointsCount int
    Kind             string  // "session" | "agent_review"
    ReviewSkills     []string
    ReviewPrompt     string
}

type SessionContent struct {
    Transcript        []byte
    Prompts           string  // full prompt.txt content (multi-turn)
    Metadata          CommittedMetadata
}
```

**Key reading methods (from `checkpoint/committed.go`):**
- `GitStore.ListCommitted()` → scans all checkpoint dirs, reads metadata
- `GitStore.ReadLatestSessionContent()` → reads full session content including prompts
- `GitStore.ReadSessionContent(ctx, cpID, sessionIndex)` → reads specific session

**Key reading methods (from `strategy/common.go`):**
- `ReadLatestSessionPromptFromCommittedTree()` → reads first prompt from prompt.txt
- `ReadAllSessionPromptsFromTree()` → reads all session prompts (multi-session)
- `ExtractFirstPrompt()` → extracts first non-empty prompt from prompt.txt content

**Sharding:** Checkpoint IDs are sharded into 256 buckets using first 2 hex chars.
Path: `a3/b2c4d5e6f7/` (from `id.CheckpointID.Path()`)

### What's Missing

- **No CLI command** to search prompt text — prompts exist in git but aren't exposed
- **No search index** — every search would need to walk all checkpoint trees
- **No ranking** — even if you could walk, there's no relevance scoring
- **Existing `entire search`** — searches code/diffs via external API, not prompts

---

## 4. Design Goals

1. **Offline-first** — works without internet, no external API dependency
2. **Git-native** — leverages existing `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch, no new storage
3. **Zero config** — works immediately, no setup required
4. **Incrementally updated** — index built once at condensation time
5. **Fast queries** — sub-second search over thousands of prompts
6. **Privacy-preserving** — PII redaction already in place, no new exposure

---

## 5. Implementation Approaches

### Approach A: On-Demand Git Tree Scan (No Index)

**How it works:**
- On every search, walk the entire/checkpoints/v1 tree and read all prompt.txt files
- No persistent index, just raw git tree traversal

**Pros:**
- Zero additional storage
- Always up-to-date (no sync needed)
- No complexity

**Cons:**
- O(n) on number of checkpoints — slow at scale
- Reads every blob on every query — expensive
- No ranking — just substring match

**Verdict:** Not acceptable. 1000 checkpoints = 1000 blob reads per search.

---

### Approach B: In-Memory Index (Built at Query Time)

**How it works:**
- On first search, read all checkpoint metadata + prompts into memory
- Cache in process, rebuild on invalidation
- Subsequent searches are in-memory

**Pros:**
- Fast queries after initial warm-up
- Simple implementation
- No disk storage

**Cons:**
- Memory grows unbounded
- Initial warm-up slow on large repos
- No persistence across CLI invocations

**Verdict:** Not ideal but acceptable for MVP. Simple, works offline, fast enough.

---

### Approach C: Persistent Local Index (File-based)

**How it works:**
- Build a persistent index stored in `.entire/prompts/` (gitignored)
- Index file stores: checkpoint ID, session ID, prompt text (truncated), timestamp, agent, files touched
- Updated incrementally at condensation time (PostCommit hook adds new entries)
- On search, read index file and filter/rank in-memory

**Pros:**
- Persistent across CLI invocations
- Fast warm-up (just read index file)
- Incremental updates (only new checkpoints added)
- Works offline, no external deps

**Cons:**
- New file in `.entire/` (gitignored, but needs management)
- Index file could grow large (mitigated by truncation + compression)
- Need to handle index invalidation on branch operations

**Verdict:** RECOMMENDED. Best balance of simplicity, performance, and UX.

---

### Approach D: SQLite FTS5 (Full-Text Search)

**How it works:**
- Store prompts in a SQLite database with FTS5 virtual table
- Use SQLite's built-in BM25 ranking

**Pros:**
- Best-in-class full-text search
- Handles large datasets well
- Mature technology

**Cons:**
- **CGO dependency** — requires `gcc` to compile sqlite3, adds complexity to builds
- Binary size increase (~2MB)
- Not already a dependency in this project
- Cross-platform build complexity

**Verdict:** Not for Phase 1. Good future option if we want advanced ranking.

---

### Approach E: External Search API (Cloud)

**How it works:**
- Push prompt index to Entire's cloud service
- Search via `entire search` command (already exists for code)

**Pros:**
- Best search quality (embeddings + BM25)
- Cross-repo search

**Cons:**
- Requires auth + internet
- Not offline-first
- Not user-owned data

**Verdict:** Not for this feature. `entire prompts` should be local-first.

---

### Chosen Approach: Approach C (Persistent Local Index)

**Summary:**
- Store index as a compressed JSON file in `.entire/prompts/index.json.gz`
- Index built/updated at PostCommit hook (condensation time)
- In-memory search with in-memory ranking
- Fallback to on-demand scan if index is missing/corrupt

**Why:**
- Simple (JSON, no new deps)
- Fast (compressed but small enough to read quickly)
- Offline-first (no API needed)
- Incremental (only new checkpoints added)
- Git-native (lives in `.entire/`, gitignored)

---

## 6. Search Algorithm

### Phase 1: Keyword Search (BM25-style)

**Algorithm:** Weighted substring matching with ranking

**Ranking formula:**
```
Score = (exact_phrase_matches * 10) + (all_words_found * 5) + (any_word_found * 1)
```

Where:
- **exact_phrase_matches**: Query as a phrase (all words adjacent in order)
- **all_words_found**: Every query word appears somewhere in the prompt
- **any_word_found**: At least one query word appears

**Tokenization:**
- Lowercase, trim
- Split on whitespace
- Remove common stop words: "the", "a", "an", "is", "are", "was", "were", "to", "of", "in", "for", "and", "or", "but"
- Support quoted phrases: `"redis cache"` treated as exact match

**Example:**
```
Query: "add redis caching"
Prompt: "Add Redis caching for session store"
→ exact match: no ("add redis caching" not contiguous)
→ all words found: yes (add, redis, caching all present)
→ score = 5
```

**Result ordering:**
1. Exact phrase matches (highest score)
2. All words found
3. Any word found
4. Within same tier: newer checkpoints first

---

## 7. Data Flow

### Index Build (at condensation / PostCommit hook)

```
User commits → PostCommit hook → Strategy.Condense()
      ↓
WriteCommitted() writes checkpoint to entire/checkpoints/v1
      ↓
condenseAndUpdateState() returns sessionData with Prompts
      ↓
PromptsIndexer.AddCheckpoint(cpID, sessionData)
      ↓
Read checkpoint metadata (Agent, Model, FilesTouched, CreatedAt, Branch)
Read prompt.txt content (truncate to 2000 chars for index)
Write index entry to .entire/prompts/index.json.gz
```

**Index entry schema:**
```go
type PromptIndex struct {
    Version   int              // index format version (1)
    UpdatedAt  time.Time        // last index update
    Checkpoints []PromptEntry  // sorted by checkpoint ID (not time)
}

type PromptEntry struct {
    CheckpointID  string    // "a3b2c4d5e6f7"
    SessionID     string    // "2026-03-15-uuid"
    PromptText    string    // truncated to 2000 chars
    Agent         string    // "Claude Code"
    Model         string    // "claude-sonnet-4-20250514"
    FilesTouched  []string  // files modified
    Branch        string    // branch name at commit time
    CreatedAt     time.Time // checkpoint creation time
}
```

### Query (at search command)

```
entire prompts search "redis cache"
      ↓
LoadIndex() — read .entire/prompts/index.json.gz into memory
      ↓
TokenizeQuery("redis cache") → ["redis", "cache"]
      ↓
Search(checkpoints, query) — rank all entries
      ↓
FormatResults() — display top 20 results with context
```

---

## 8. Command Interface

### `entire prompts search <query>`

**Usage:**
```
entire prompts search <query>          # Search prompts
entire prompts search "redis cache"    # Search for specific terms
entire prompts search --limit 50       # Show more results
entire prompts search --json           # JSON output
entire prompts search --agent claude   # Filter by agent
entire prompts search --branch feat/x  # Filter by branch
entire prompts search --after 2026-03  # Filter by date
```

**Output format:**
```

  "Why did we choose Redis over Memcached for the caching layer?"

  7f8e9d1a2b3c  2026-04-02  Gemini CLI   feat/cache
  "Add Redis caching for session store to improve latency"

  f1e2d3c4b5a6  2026-04-15  Claude Code  main
  "Migrate in-memory cache to Redis cluster for production"
```

**With `--json`:**
```json

  "total": 23,
  "results": [
    {
      "checkpoint_id": "a3b2c4d5e6f7",

      "branch": "main",

      "score": 8
    }
  ]

```

### `entire prompts list`

**Usage:**
```

entire prompts list --limit 50       # Show more
entire prompts list --checkpoint abc # Show prompts for specific checkpoint
```

### `entire prompts show <checkpoint-id>`

**Usage:**
```

entire prompts show abc123             # Short prefix accepted
```

**Output format:**
```

Branch: main
Created: 2026-03-15 10:30:00

  cache/redis.go

---

## 9. Component Design

### Package Structure

```
cmd/entire/cli/prompts/
├── prompts.go       # Main command group + subcommands
├── search.go        # Search command implementation
├── list.go          # List command implementation
├── show.go          # Show command implementation
├── index.go         # Index build/update logic
├── store.go         # Index file I/O (read/write .entire/prompts/)
├── rank.go          # Ranking algorithm
├── test/
│   ├── prompts_test.go
│   ├── search_test.go
│   └── rank_test.go
```

### Index Store (`store.go`)

**Location:** `.entire/prompts/index.json.gz`
- Gitignored (contains local session data)
- Compressed with gzip to reduce disk usage
- Atomic writes (write to temp file, rename)

**Operations:**
- `LoadIndex(path string) (*PromptIndex, error)` — read index
- `SaveIndex(path string, idx *PromptIndex) error` — write index
- `IndexPath(repoRoot string) string` — get `.entire/prompts/index.json.gz`

### Ranker (`rank.go`)

**Operations:**
- `ScoreEntry(entry PromptEntry, query string) float64` — score single entry
- `TokenizeQuery(query string) []string` — tokenize search query
- `TokenizePrompt(prompt string) []string` — tokenize prompt for matching
- `Search(index *PromptIndex, query string, limit int) []SearchResult` — find matching entries

### Hook Integration

The index is updated at condensation time (PostCommit hook in `manual_commit_hooks.go`).
New code in `prompts/index.go`:
```go
func (idx *PromptIndex) AddCheckpoint(cpID string, session SessionData) error
```

Called from the PostCommit hook handler after `writeCommitted` succeeds.

---

## 10. Benchmarking

### Target Performance

| Operation | Target | Notes |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Index load (100 checkpoints) | < 50ms | Compressed JSON, ~50KB |
| Index load (1000 checkpoints) | < 200ms | Compressed JSON, ~500KB |
| Index load (10000 checkpoints) | < 1s | Compressed JSON, ~5MB |
| Search query (100 checkpoints) | < 10ms | In-memory, no I/O |
| Search query (1000 checkpoints) | < 50ms | In-memory, no I/O |
| Search query (10000 checkpoints) | < 200ms | In-memory, no I/O |
| Index build (new checkpoint) | < 100ms | Append to existing index |

### Index Size Estimates

| Checkpoints | Avg prompt length | Index size (compressed) |
|-------------|-------------------|-------------------------|
| 100 | 200 chars | ~50KB |
| 1,000 | 200 chars | ~500KB |
| 10,000 | 200 chars | ~5MB |
| 100,000 | 200 chars | ~50MB |

### Comparison: Index vs No Index

| Checkpoints | On-demand scan | Indexed search |
|-------------|----------------|----------------|
| 100 | ~500ms | < 10ms |
| 1,000 | ~5s | < 50ms |
| 10,000 | ~50s | < 200ms |

**On-demand scan is not acceptable at scale. Index is required.**

---

## 11. Edge Cases

### 1. Missing index file
- On first run, no index exists
- Fall back to on-demand git tree scan
- Build index in background, warn user results may be incomplete

### 2. Corrupt index file
- Detect via JSON parse error or magic bytes mismatch
- Delete corrupt file, rebuild from git tree
- Log warning: "Index corrupted, rebuilding..."

### 3. Large prompts
- Truncate prompt text to 2000 chars in index
- Full prompt available via `entire prompts show <checkpoint-id>` (reads from git)

### 4. Multi-session checkpoints
- Index all sessions separately (0/, 1/, 2/)
- Each session prompt gets its own entry
- Display session index in results: "Session 2 of 3"

### 5. Empty prompts
- Skip checkpoints with empty or whitespace-only prompts
- Log count of skipped (for debugging)

### 6. Non-ASCII prompts
- Full UTF-8 support required
- Tokenization respects Unicode word boundaries
- Stop words: English only (expandable)

### 7. Checkpoint deleted from git
- Index still contains old checkpoint IDs
- On access, check if checkpoint exists in git
- If not found, skip in search results (don't delete from index on every query)

### 8. Branch renaming / rebasing
- Branch name is metadata only, not used for sharding
- Checkpoint ID is stable across branch operations
- No invalidation needed

### 9. Privacy / PII
- Prompts stored in git are already redacted (PII redaction at condensation time)
- Index uses same prompt content as git storage
- No new data exposure

### 10. Cross-repo search
- Not supported in Phase 1
- Future: sync index to checkpoint remote, search across repos

---

## 12. Implementation Plan

### Phase 1: Core (MVP)

**Week 1:**
- Create `cmd/entire/cli/prompts/` package
- Implement index store (`store.go`) — read/write compressed JSON
- Implement index builder (`index.go`) — addCheckpoint from session data
- Implement ranker (`rank.go`) — keyword matching + scoring
- Add PostCommit hook integration to update index

**Week 2:**
- Implement `entire prompts list` command
- Implement `entire prompts search` command
- Implement `entire prompts show` command
- Add basic tests

**Week 3:**
- Add `--limit`, `--agent`, `--branch`, `--after` filters
- Add `--json` output
- Add interactive mode (Bubble Tea TUI)
- Performance testing and optimization

### Phase 2: Enhanced (Future)

- Add TF-IDF ranking for better relevance
- Add file context in results (show which files prompt touched)
- Add session threading (show multi-turn conversations)
- Performance optimization (lazy loading, pagination)

### Phase 3: Semantic (Future)

- Add embedding generation (local or API)
- Implement hybrid search (BM25 + dense retrieval)
- Add privacy controls (exclude sensitive repos)

---

## 13. Open Questions

1. **Index rebuild on migration?** — If user migrates from v1 to v2 checkpoints, should we rebuild index?
2. **Prompt truncation length?** — 2000 chars is an estimate. What's the real distribution?
3. **Stop word list?** — English stop words only for now. Add more languages later?
4. **Interactive mode?** — Bubble Tea TUI for search with pager, or stick to CLI output?
5. **Integration with `entire search`?** — Should `entire search --prompts` delegate to this?

---

## 14. Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `entire prompts search <query>` returns relevant prompts in < 200ms for 10K checkpoints
- [ ] `entire prompts list` shows recent prompts with checkpoint IDs
- [ ] `entire prompts show <checkpoint-id>` shows full prompt text
- [ ] Index is updated automatically on every commit
- [ ] Works offline without internet
- [ ] No new external dependencies (no CGO, no SQLite)
- [ ] Tests cover ranking algorithm and edge cases
- [ ] Performance: index load < 1s for 10K checkpoints

---

1. [Entire Roadmap Blog](https://entire.io/blog/the-entire-cli-how-it-works-and-where-its-headed)
2. `checkpoint/checkpoint.go` — Checkpoint types

1: # Contributing to the Entire CLI
2: 
3: Thank you for your interest in contributing to Entire! We welcome contributions from everyone.
4: 
5: Please read our [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) before participating.
6: 
7: > **New to Entire?** See the [README](README.md) for setup and usage documentation.

9: ---
10: 
11: ## Before You Code: Discuss First
12: 
13: The fastest way to get a contribution merged is to align with maintainers before writing code. Please **open an issue first** using our [issue templates](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues/new/choose) and wait for maintainer feedback before starting implementation.
14: 
15: ### Contribution Workflow
16: 
17: 1. **Open an issue** describing the problem or feature
18: 2. **Wait for maintainer feedback** -- we may have relevant context or plans
19: 3. **Get approval** before starting implementation
20: 4. **Submit your PR** referencing the approved issue

22: 6. **Maintainer review and merge**

30: ### Good First Issues

32: We recommend starting with:
33: - **Documentation improvements** - Fix typos, clarify explanations, add examples

48: 
49: If you discover a security vulnerability, **do not report it through GitHub Issues**. Instead, please follow the instructions in our [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) file for responsible disclosure. All security reports are kept confidential as described in SECURITY.md.

57: - [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues) - Bug reports and feature requests

60: Please represent the project and community respectfully in all public and private interactions.

63: ## How to Contribute
64: 
65: 
66: There are many ways to contribute:
67: 
68: - **Feature requests** - Open a [GitHub Issue](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues) to discuss your idea
69: - **Bug reports** - Report issues via [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/entireio/cli/issues) (see [Reporting Bugs](#reporting-bugs))

75: ## Reporting Bugs
76: 
77: Good bug reports help us fix issues quickly. When reporting a bug, please include:
78: 
79: ### Required Information
80: 
81: 1. **Entire CLI version** - run `entire version`
82: 2. **Operating system**
83: 3. **Go version** - run `go version`
84: 
85: ### What to Include
86: 
87: Please answer these questions in your bug report:
88: 
89: 1. **What did you do?** - Include the exact commands you ran
90: 2. **What did you expect to happen?**
91: 3. **What actually happened?** - Include the full error message or unexpected output
92: 4. **Can you reproduce it?** - Does it happen every time or intermittently?
93: 5. **Any additional context?** - Logs, screenshots, or related issues

181: ## Creating an Agent
182: 
183: 
184: Entire supports two ways to create agents:
185: 
186: ### 1. Claude Code Agent Personas (Markdown)
187: 
188: These are markdown files that define specialized behaviors for Claude Code (e.g., developer, reviewer, etc.).
189: 
190: - **Location:** `.claude/agents/`
191: - **Structure:**
192:    ```markdown
193:    ---
194:    name: my-agent
195:    description: What this agent does
196:    model: opus
197:    color: blue
198:    ---
199: 
200:    # Agent Name
201:    You are a **[Role]** with expertise in [domain].

205:    - Principle 2
206: 
207:    ## Process
208:    1. Step 1
209:    2. Step 2
210: 
211:    ## Output Format

214: - **To invoke:** Create a matching command in `.claude/commands/` that spawns the agent via the Task tool.
215: - **Examples:**
216:    - `.claude/agents/dev.md` - TDD Developer
217:    - `.claude/agents/reviewer.md` - Code Reviewer
218: 
219: ### 2. Coding Agent Integrations (Go)
220: 
221: These are Go implementations that integrate Entire with different AI coding tools (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, Copilot CLI, etc.) using the Agent abstraction layer.
222: 
223: - **Location:** `cmd/entire/cli/agent/`
224: - **Steps:**
225:    1. Implement the `Agent` interface in `agent/agent.go`
226:    2. Register your agent in the agent registry
227:    3. Add setup and hook configuration as needed
228:    4. Ensure session and checkpoint tracking is handled per the abstraction
229: - **Reference:** See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for architecture and code examples.

233: **Which should I use?**
234: 
235: - Use a persona markdown agent if you want to create a new role or workflow for Claude Code.
236: - Use a coding agent integration if you want to add support for a new AI coding tool or extend agent capabilities in the CLI.

240: ## Submitting a Pull Request
241: 
242: ### Before You Submit
243: 
244: - **Related issue exists and is approved** -- Your PR references an issue where a maintainer has acknowledged the approach. (Exceptions: documentation fixes, typo corrections, and `good-first-issue` items.)
245: - **Linting passes** -- Run `mise run lint` (includes golangci-lint, gofmt, gomod, shellcheck)
246: - **Tests pass** -- Run `mise run test` to verify your changes

253: 
254: 1. **Push** your branch to your fork

262: ## Responding to Automated Review
263: 
264: Co-pilot agent reviews every PR and provides feedback on code quality, potential bugs, and project conventions.
265: 
266: **Read and respond to every Copilot comment.** PRs with unaddressed Copilot feedback will not move to maintainer review.
267: 
268: - **Fixed** -- Push a commit addressing the issue.
269: - **Disagree** -- Reply explaining your reasoning. The Copilot isn't always right.
270: - **Question** -- Ask for clarification. We're happy to help.

272: Addressing Copilot feedback upfront is the fastest path to maintainer review.

276: ## Using Entire While Contributing
277: 
278: We use Entire on Entire. When contributing, install the Entire CLI and let it capture your coding sessions -- this gives us valuable dogfooding data and helps improve the tool.
279: 
280: ### Setup
281: 
282: Install the latest version of the Entire CLI (see [installation docs](https://docs.entire.io/cli/installation)) and verify with `entire version`. Entire is already configured in this repository, so there's no need to run `entire enable`.
283: 
284: ### Checkpoint Trailers
285: 
286: All commits should include `Entire-Checkpoint` trailers from your sessions. These are added automatically by the `prepare-commit-msg` hook when Entire is enabled. The trailers link your commits to session metadata on the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch.

289: 
290: When you push your PR branch, Entire can automatically push the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch alongside it (if `push_sessions` is enabled in your settings). Include this in your PR so maintainers can review the session context behind your changes.

# Feature Proposal: `entire prompts search` — Searchable Prompt History

**Roadmap:** https://entire.io/blog/the-entire-cli-how-it-works-and-where-its-headed  
**Status:** Not shipped, not in progress  
**Updated:** May 2026

---

## 1. Problem Statement

> "We're making that answer searchable. Users will be able to surface the prompt that introduced a workaround or revisit the reasoning behind a library choice months later. The 'why' will be part of your history." — Entire Roadmap

Developers can search **what changed** (`git blame`, `grep`) but cannot search **why it changed** — the prompts and reasoning behind decisions. Today that context lives in closed terminal sessions and disappears on close.

**Example:** "Why did we pick Redis over Memcached?"
- `grep redis` → finds usage, not decision
- `git blame` → shows who changed it, not why
- Slack / Notion → fragmented, not tied to commits
- Ask teammates → unreliable, doesn't scale

**With searchable prompts:**
```
$ entire prompts search "cache decision"
→ "Why did we choose Redis over Memcached?"   a3b2c4d5e6f7  2026-03-15  Claude Code
→ "Add Redis caching for session store"        7f8e9d1a2b3c  2026-04-02  Gemini CLI
```

---

## 2. Roadmap Alignment

| Feature | Status | Roadmap Section |
|---|---|---|
| **Searchable Prompts** | NOT SHIPPED | "Search" — surfacing the prompt that introduced a workaround |
| Intent Review | NOT SHIPPED | "Rethinking Code Review to Intent Review" |
| Team Visibility | NOT SHIPPED | "Team Visibility" |
| Audit & Transparency | Partial | Line-level attribution exists |

This proposal covers **only Searchable Prompts**. Intent review and team visibility are separate tracks.

---

## 3. Current Architecture

### What Already Exists

```
Checkpoint Condensation
      ↓
GitStore.WriteCommitted()
      ↓
entire/checkpoints/v1 branch
      ↓
<checkpoint-id[:2]>/<checkpoint-id[2:]>/
├── metadata.json           # CheckpointSummary (no prompts)
├── 0/                      # Session 0
│   ├── metadata.json       # CommittedMetadata
│   ├── full.jsonl          # Full transcript
│   └── prompt.txt          # User prompts (multi-turn, split by "---\n\n")
├── 1/                      # Session 1 (multi-session)
...
```

**Key types (`checkpoint/checkpoint.go`):**
```go
type CheckpointSummary struct {
    CheckpointID  id.CheckpointID
    Sessions      []SessionFilePaths
    FilesTouched  []string
    HasReview     bool
}

type CommittedMetadata struct {
    SessionID        string
    Agent            types.AgentType
    Model            string
    CreatedAt        time.Time
    CheckpointsCount int
    Kind             string   // "session" | "agent_review"
    ReviewSkills     []string
    ReviewPrompt     string   // NOTE: agent review prompts also live here
}
```

**Key reading methods (`checkpoint/committed.go`):**
- `GitStore.ListCommitted()` — scans all checkpoint dirs, reads metadata
- `GitStore.ReadSessionContent(ctx, cpID, sessionIndex)` — reads specific session including prompt.txt
- `GitStore.ReadLatestSessionContent()` — reads most recent session

**Key reading methods (`strategy/common.go`):**
- `ReadAllSessionPromptsFromTree()` — reads all session prompts (multi-session aware)
- `ExtractFirstPrompt()` — extracts first non-empty turn from prompt.txt

**Sharding:** Checkpoint IDs sharded into 256 buckets via first 2 hex chars. Path: `a3/b2c4d5e6f7/`.

### What's Missing

- No CLI command exposing prompt text to users
- No search index — every query would need a full git tree walk
- No ranking — no relevance scoring over results
- Existing `entire search` hits an external API for code/diffs; prompts are local and offline-first

---

## 4. Design Goals

1. **Offline-first** — works without internet, no external API dependency
2. **Git-native** — leverages existing `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch, no new storage layer
3. **Zero config** — works immediately after `entire enable`, no setup required
4. **Incrementally updated** — index written at condensation time, never requires a full rebuild in steady state
5. **Fast queries** — sub-200ms for 10K checkpoints
6. **Privacy-preserving** — uses only the already-redacted prompt content from checkpoint storage

---

## 5. What This Proposal Does NOT Cover

To be explicit about scope:
- No cross-repo search (Phase 3+)
- No semantic/embedding search (Phase 3+)
- No integration with the web platform (separate feature)
- No multi-language stop words (English only in Phase 1)
- No real-time index — index is commit-time only

---

## 6. Implementation Approach

### Approach Comparison

| | A: On-demand scan | B: In-memory (query time) | **C: Persistent local index** | D: SQLite FTS5 | E: Cloud API |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Offline | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| Fast queries | ❌ 50s/1K | ⚠️ slow cold start | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Incremental | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| No new deps | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ CGO | ✅ |
| Persistent | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

**Chosen: Approach C — Persistent Local Index**

A persistent index stored as newline-delimited JSON (`.ndjson`) in `.entire/prompts/index.ndjson`, updated incrementally at condensation time via the PostCommit hook.

**Why `.ndjson` over `.json.gz`:**
gzip is a stream format — you cannot append to it. Every update would require read → decompress → deserialize → modify → compress → rewrite the entire file. `.ndjson` is truly appendable: new entries are written as a single line append. No full rewrites, no decompression overhead. At 5MB for 10K checkpoints, compression is not necessary.

---

## 7. Index Design

### File Location

```
.entire/prompts/index.ndjson    # gitignored, local to this checkout
```

**Decoupled repo support:** When checkpoints are stored in a separate repository (`checkpoint.remote` config), the index lives alongside the checkpoints — in that repo's working directory — not in the main repo. `IndexPath()` reads the checkpoint store config before resolving.

**Multi-worktree support:** Each worktree has its own `.git` directory. The index lives at `<worktree-git-dir>/../.entire/prompts/index.ndjson`, not at the repo root, so concurrent worktrees have independent indexes that don't collide.

### Schema

Each line in the `.ndjson` file is one JSON object:

```go
type PromptEntry struct {
    // Identity
    CheckpointID    string    `json:"checkpoint_id"`    // "a3b2c4d5e6f7"
    SessionIndex    int       `json:"session_index"`    // 0, 1, 2 (multi-session)
    TurnIndex       int       `json:"turn_index"`       // 0, 1, 2 (multi-turn within session)
    Kind            string    `json:"kind"`             // "session" | "agent_review"

    // Prompt content
    PromptText      string    `json:"prompt_text"`      // truncated to 2000 chars
    PromptTruncated bool      `json:"prompt_truncated"` // true if original was longer

    // Git context
    CommitHash      string    `json:"commit_hash"`      // git commit SHA
    CommitMessage   string    `json:"commit_message"`   // first line only
    Branch          string    `json:"branch"`           // branch at commit time

    // Agent metadata
    Agent           string    `json:"agent"`            // "Claude Code"
    Model           string    `json:"model"`            // "claude-sonnet-4-20250514"
    TokenCount      int       `json:"token_count"`      // from CommittedMetadata

    // Subagent context
    ParentCheckpointID string `json:"parent_checkpoint_id,omitempty"` // set for subagents
    SubagentDepth      int    `json:"subagent_depth"`                 // 0 = top-level

    // Useful for filtering
    FilesTouched    []string  `json:"files_touched"`
    CreatedAt       time.Time `json:"created_at"`
}

// Index header — first line of the file
type IndexHeader struct {
    Version   int       `json:"version"`    // format version (1)
    CreatedAt time.Time `json:"created_at"`
    RepoRoot  string    `json:"repo_root"`  // sanity check on load
}
```

**Why `TurnIndex` matters:** `prompt.txt` stores multi-turn conversations separated by `"---\n\n"`. Each turn is indexed as a separate `PromptEntry` (same `CheckpointID`, incrementing `TurnIndex`). This ensures "Why did we choose Redis?" matches even if it appears in turn 3 of a 5-turn session, not just in the first message.

**Why `ReviewPrompt` is included:** `CommittedMetadata.ReviewPrompt` holds the prompt used for agent reviews (`kind: "agent_review"`). These prompts represent intent just as much as user prompts do and should be searchable. They are indexed with `Kind: "agent_review"` so users can filter them.

**Why `CommitHash` and `CommitMessage`:** These link a search result back to the actual git commit, enabling `git show <hash>` or navigation to the diff. Without them, a search result has no path back to the code change it produced.

**Why `TokenCount`:** Entire already tracks token usage per session. Surfacing it in search results (and eventually in team visibility) is zero-cost since the data exists.

### Index Version Migration

```go
const CurrentIndexVersion = 1

func LoadIndex(path string) (*PromptIndex, error) {
    // Read header (first line)
    if header.Version < CurrentIndexVersion {
        return nil, ErrIndexVersionMismatch // triggers rebuild
    }
    if header.Version > CurrentIndexVersion {
        return nil, ErrIndexTooNew // CLI needs update
    }
    // ...
}
```

On `ErrIndexVersionMismatch`, the CLI deletes the old index and triggers a full rebuild automatically.

---

## 8. Concurrent Write Safety

The existing architecture supports concurrent sessions (two agents in the same repo simultaneously). Two simultaneous PostCommit hooks writing to the index file without coordination will silently overwrite each other.

**Solution: advisory file lock**

```go
func (s *IndexStore) AppendEntry(entry PromptEntry) error {
    lock, err := lockfile.New(s.LockPath()) // .entire/prompts/index.lock
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    if err := lock.TryLock(); err != nil {
        // Another hook is writing; retry with backoff (max 3 attempts, 50ms apart)
        return s.retryAppend(entry, 3)
    }
    defer lock.Unlock()
    return s.appendLine(entry)
}
```

**NFS note:** `flock` is unreliable on NFS-mounted `.git` directories. We detect NFS mounts via `statfs` and fall back to a `.lock` file with a PID-based ownership check, same pattern used by git itself.

## 9. Search Algorithm

### Tokenizer

```go
func Tokenize(text string) []string {
    // 1. Unicode normalization (NFC) — "café" == "cafe\u0301" after normalize
    normalized := norm.NFC.String(strings.ToLower(text))
    // 2. Split on non-word characters
    tokens := wordBoundary.Split(normalized, -1)
    // 3. Stem each token (Porter stemmer, pure Go, no CGO)
    //    "caching" → "cache", "authenticated" → "authent", "decisions" → "decis"
    stemmed := make([]string, 0, len(tokens))
    for _, t := range tokens {
        if len(t) < 2 { continue }           // skip single chars
        if stopWords[t] { continue }          // skip stop words
        stemmed = append(stemmed, stem.Stem(t))
    }
    return stemmed
}
```

**Stemmer:** `github.com/kljensen/snowball` — pure Go, zero CGO, MIT licensed. Not currently a dependency; adding it is a single `go get`.

**Why stemming matters for recall:**
- `"caching"` → stems to `"cach"` → matches prompt containing `"cache"`, `"cached"`, `"caches"`
- `"authenticated"` → stems to `"authent"` → matches `"auth"`, `"authentication"`
- Without stemming roughly 30–40% of valid matches return zero results

### Scoring

Weighted keyword scoring with term-density normalization. This is **not** BM25 (which requires IDF across a corpus). It is honest keyword scoring appropriate for a local index of this size:

```
TermDensity = matched_token_count / total_prompt_token_count

Score = (exact_phrase_match * 10)
      + (all_query_tokens_found * 5)
      + (any_query_token_found * 1)
      + (TermDensity * 2)        ← prevents long prompts from dominating
```

**Result ordering within same score tier:** newer `CreatedAt` first.

**Minimum query length:** Queries shorter than 2 characters after tokenization return an error: `"query too short — enter at least one word"`. This prevents accidental full-index scans from single-char queries.

**Special character handling:** Query strings are stripped of regex metacharacters (`$`, `*`, `.`, `+`, `?`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `^`, `|`, `\`) before tokenization. They are not interpreted as patterns. This prevents panics and confusing zero-result queries.

**Quoted phrase handling:** `"redis cache"` is parsed as a phrase and matched as an adjacent sequence in the stemmed token stream. Phrase matches score as `exact_phrase_match`.

## 10. Cold Start and Index Rebuild

**The problem:** On first install, or when a user points Entire at an existing repo with hundreds of checkpoints, the index doesn't exist. The current proposal falls back to on-demand git tree scan which takes ~50s for 1000 checkpoints — an unusable first experience.

**Solution: explicit rebuild command with progress**

```
$ entire prompts index --rebuild
Building prompt index from 847 checkpoints...
████████████████████░░░░  780/847  (92%)  ETA 3s

Done. Indexed 1,623 prompts from 847 checkpoints.
Index written to .entire/prompts/index.ndjson (412 KB)
```

The rebuild command:
1. Walks `entire/checkpoints/v1` tree in the git object store
2. Reads each session's `prompt.txt` (multi-turn aware)
3. Reads `ReviewPrompt` from `metadata.json` where `kind == "agent_review"`
4. Writes a fresh `index.ndjson` atomically (temp file + rename)

**Auto-trigger on first search:** If the index is missing and the user runs `entire prompts search`, the CLI triggers a rebuild automatically with a one-line notice: `"Building prompt index for the first time..."`. Subsequent queries are fast.

**`entire prompts index` subcommands:**

```
entire prompts index --rebuild    # full rebuild from git tree
entire prompts index --status     # show index health and stats
entire prompts index --verify     # check all indexed checkpoint IDs still exist in git
```

`--status` output:

## 13. Data Flow

### Index update (at condensation — PostCommit hook)

```
User commits → PostCommit hook fires
      ↓
strategy.Condense() → WriteCommitted() writes checkpoint to git
      ↓
For each session in checkpoint:
    Read prompt.txt → split on "---\n\n" → each turn = one PromptEntry
    Read CommittedMetadata → Agent, Model, TokenCount, Kind, ReviewPrompt
    Read CommitHash and CommitMessage from git HEAD
    Truncate prompt to 2000 chars (set PromptTruncated = true if over)
      ↓
Acquire file lock on index.lock
Append new PromptEntry lines to index.ndjson
Release lock
```

### Query (at search command)

```
entire prompts search "redis cache"
      ↓
LoadIndex() — read index.ndjson line by line into []PromptEntry
  If missing → trigger rebuild → reload
  If version mismatch → rebuild → reload
      ↓
ParseQuery("redis cache") → handle quotes, strip special chars
TokenizeQuery() → stem tokens, remove stop words
      ↓
Score each PromptEntry (in-memory, no I/O after load)
      ↓
Apply filters (--agent, --branch, --after, --files, --kind)
Sort by score desc, then CreatedAt desc
Slice to --limit
      ↓
FormatResults() → TTY output or JSON
```

## 14. Edge Cases

| # | Case | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Missing index | Auto-trigger rebuild with progress bar; warn results may lag until complete |
| 2 | Corrupt index (parse error) | Delete, rebuild, log: `"Prompt index corrupt, rebuilding..."` |
| 3 | Index version mismatch | Delete, rebuild automatically |
| 4 | Large prompts (>2000 chars) | Truncate in index; `entire prompts show` reads full content from git |
| 5 | Match past truncation point | If query matches but was truncated, result still shown with note: `"(prompt truncated — run 'entire prompts show' for full text)"` |
| 6 | Multi-turn conversations | Each turn indexed as separate `PromptEntry` with `TurnIndex` |
| 7 | Agent review prompts | Indexed with `Kind: "agent_review"`, searchable, filterable with `--kind` |
| 8 | Subagent checkpoints | Each subagent checkpoint indexed with `ParentCheckpointID` and `SubagentDepth` |
| 9 | Empty prompts | Skipped; count logged in `--status` output |
| 10 | Non-ASCII / Unicode | NFC normalization before tokenization; `"café"` matches `"cafe"` |
| 11 | Special chars in query | Stripped before tokenization; not interpreted as regex |
| 12 | Query too short (<2 chars) | Early return with: `"query too short — enter at least one word"` |
| 13 | Checkpoint deleted from git | `--verify` identifies orphans; search skips them silently |
| 14 | `git gc` pruning objects | Same as above — orphan detection handles it |
| 15 | Concurrent writes (two agents) | File lock with retry backoff; NFS fallback to PID-lock file |
| 16 | Multiple worktrees | Index path is worktree-local (`<worktree-git-dir>/../.entire/`) |
| 17 | Decoupled checkpoint repo | `IndexPath()` reads checkpoint store config to resolve location |
| 18 | Windows path separators | `FilesTouched` entries normalized to forward slashes in index |
| 19 | Git LFS checkpoints | Detect LFS pointer format in blobs; log warning and skip rather than index raw pointer text |
| 20 | NFS filesystem | `statfs` detection → PID-lock file fallback instead of `flock` |
| 21 | Branch rename / rebase | Checkpoint IDs are stable; branch name is metadata only |
| 22 | Prefix ambiguity in `show` | List matching IDs and prompt user to disambiguate |
| 23 | `--json` in non-TTY | Warn to stderr: sensitive prompt text in output |
| 24 | PII across agents | Document which agents run redaction at condensation time; surface in `--status` |

## 15. Benchmarks

### Target Performance

| Operation | Target | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Index load — 1K checkpoints | < 100ms | ndjson line-by-line, ~500KB |
| Index load — 10K checkpoints | < 500ms | ~5MB |
| Search query — 1K checkpoints | < 20ms | in-memory after load |
| Search query — 10K checkpoints | < 100ms | in-memory after load |
| Index append (new checkpoint) | < 50ms | single line append + file lock |
| Full rebuild — 1K checkpoints | < 10s | git tree walk + blob reads |

### Index Size Estimates

| Checkpoints | Avg prompt (chars) | `.ndjson` size |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 500 | ~650 KB |
| 10,000 | 500 | ~6.5 MB |
| 100,000 | 500 | ~65 MB |

At 100K+ checkpoints a compaction strategy (archiving old entries) should be introduced. Out of scope for Phase 1.

### On-demand scan vs indexed

| Checkpoints | On-demand scan | Indexed search |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | ~500ms | < 10ms |
| 1,000 | ~5s | < 20ms |
| 10,000 | ~50s | < 100ms |

On-demand scan is not acceptable at scale. The index is required even for moderate repos.

## 18. Open Questions

1. **Unified `entire search`?** Should `entire search` eventually become an umbrella that queries both code (external API) and prompts (local index) in one command? Fragmented search commands create UX debt. Worth a brief discussion before this ships to avoid a harder migration later.

2. **Rebuild progress UX:** What progress indicator pattern is already in use in the CLI? Should we use the existing Bubble Tea components or a simple `fmt.Printf` progress line?

3. **Index on the web platform?** Dispatch 0x000C shipped Dispatches on Entire Web. Should the prompt index eventually sync to the web platform for cross-machine search? If yes, the schema should be forward-compatible. No action needed in Phase 1, but worth flagging.

4. **Prompt truncation length?** 2000 chars is an estimate. What is the real p95 prompt length in existing checkpoint data? This affects index size estimates and whether truncation is common enough to warrant a warning in results.

5. **Which agents run PII redaction at condensation?** The proposal assumes PII is already redacted. We should verify this is true for all supported agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Factory AI Droid, OpenCode, Codex) before shipping. Any agent without redaction should be flagged in the index entry and surfaced in `--status`.

## Proposed Solution

**New command family:**
```
entire prompts search <query>   # Search prompts by keywords
entire prompts list            # List recent prompts
entire prompts show <id>       # Show full prompt for a checkpoint

```

**Implementation approach:** Persistent local index (`.ndjson` in `.entire/prompts/`) — offline-first, no new external deps, no CGO.

### Key design decisions:

- **Storage:** `.ndjson` (newline-delimited JSON) — appendable, no compression overhead, ~650KB for 1K checkpoints
- **Algorithm:** Porter stemmer (pure Go, `github.com/kljensen/snowball`) + weighted keyword scoring. Not BM25 (requires IDF across corpus; overkill for local index)
- **Index update:** At PostCommit hook (condensation time) — incrementally updated, never requires a full rebuild in steady state
- **Cold start:** `entire prompts index --rebuild` walks `entire/checkpoints/v1` git tree with a progress bar. Auto-triggers on first search if index is missing.
- **Multi-turn:** `prompt.txt` stores multi-turn conversations split by `"---\n\n"`. Each turn is indexed as a separate entry with `TurnIndex`
- **Agent review prompts:** `CommittedMetadata.ReviewPrompt` is also indexed with `Kind: "agent_review"`
- **Concurrency:** File lock with retry backoff for concurrent writes. NFS fallback to PID-lock file.
- **Benchmarks:** Search < 20ms for 1K, < 100ms for 10K. Index load < 100ms for 1K.

| Checkpoints | On-demand scan | Indexed search |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | ~500ms | < 10ms |
| 1,000 | ~5s | < 20ms |
| 10,000 | ~50s | < 100ms |

27: shortcuts remain functional but hidden, and emit a deprecation hint pointing
28: at the canonical group form.
29: 
30: - `session` (alias: `sessions`): `list`, `info`, `stop`, `attach`, `resume`, `current`
31: - `checkpoint` (aliases: `cp`, `checkpoints`): `list`, `explain`, `rewind`, `search`
32: - `agent`: bare opens the interactive agent selector, plus `list`, `add`, `remove`
33: - `configure`: bare prints help and a hint pointing at `entire agent`; flags
34:   manage non-agent settings (telemetry, git-hook installation mode, strategy
35:   options, summary provider). Agent CRUD lives under `entire agent`.
36: - `auth`: `login`, `logout`, `status`, `list`, `revoke`
37: - `doctor`: bare runs the scan-and-fix flow, plus `trace`, `logs`, `bundle`
38: 
39: Top-level lifecycle and standalone commands: `enable`, `disable`, `status`,
40: `login`, `logout`, `clean`, `version`, `dispatch`, `activity`, `help`,
41: `configure`.
42: 
43: Hidden top-level shortcuts (functional, emit a one-line deprecation hint):
44: `rewind` → `checkpoint rewind`, `resume` → `session resume`, `attach` →
45: `session attach`, `explain` → `checkpoint explain`, `trace` → `doctor trace`.
46: Cobra-native aliases (no hint): `sessions` → `session`, `cp`/`checkpoints` →
47: `checkpoint`. The `search` top-level remains hidden without a hint.
48: 
49: Deprecated top-level alias (functional, prints cobra deprecation message):
50: `reset` → `clean`.
51: 
52: Hidden infrastructure commands: `hooks`, `migrate`, `trail`,
53: `curl-bash-post-install`, `__send_analytics`.
54: 
55: The `hideAsAlias(cmd, canonical)` helper in `cmd/entire/cli/aliascmd.go`
56: marks a command Hidden and sets cobra's `Deprecated` field so the hint
57: renders to stderr on every invocation while the command stays functional.
58: Diagnostic subcommands live alongside `doctor.go` as `doctor_logs.go` and
59: `doctor_bundle.go`. Group roots and noun-group children live in files
60: named `<noun>_group.go` and `<noun>_<verb>.go` respectively.

82: ### Running All Tests (CI)
83: 
84: ```bash
85: mise run test:ci
86: ```
87: 
88: This runs unit tests, integration tests, and the E2E canary (Vogon agent) in sequence. Integration tests use the `//go:build integration` build tag and are located in `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`.

90: ### Running E2E Canary Tests (Vogon Agent)
91: 
92: The Vogon agent is a deterministic fake agent that exercises the full E2E test suite without making any API calls. Named after the Vogons from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy — bureaucratic, procedural, and deterministic to a fault.
93: 
94: ```bash
95: mise run test:e2e:canary           # Run all E2E tests with the Vogon agent
96: mise run test:e2e:canary TestFoo   # Run a specific test
97: ```
98: 
99: - **Runs as part of `test:ci`** — canary failures block merges
100: - **No API calls, no cost** — safe to run freely, unlike real agent E2E tests
101: - **If a canary test fails, the bug is in the CLI or test infrastructure**, not in an agent
102: - Located in `e2e/vogon/` (binary) and `cmd/entire/cli/agent/vogon/` (Agent interface)
103: - The binary parses prompts via regex, creates/modifies/deletes files, and fires lifecycle hooks
104: - **IMPORTANT: When changing E2E test prompt wording**, the Vogon binary (`e2e/vogon/main.go`) parses prompts with hardcoded regexes. New phrasing may not match existing patterns — always run `mise run test:e2e:canary` after changing prompt text and fix Vogon's parsing if tests fail.
105: 
106: ### Running E2E Tests (Only When Explicitly Requested)
107: 
108: **IMPORTANT: Do NOT run E2E tests proactively.** E2E tests make real API calls to agents, which consume tokens and cost money. Only run them when the user explicitly asks for E2E testing.
109: 
110: ```bash
111: mise run test:e2e [filter]                          # All agents, filtered
112: mise run test:e2e --agent claude-code [filter]       # Claude Code only
113: mise run test:e2e --agent gemini-cli [filter]        # Gemini CLI only
114: mise run test:e2e --agent opencode [filter]          # OpenCode only
115: mise run test:e2e --agent cursor [filter]            # Cursor only
116: mise run test:e2e --agent factoryai-droid [filter]   # Factory AI Droid only
117: mise run test:e2e --agent copilot-cli [filter]       # Copilot CLI only
118: mise run test:e2e --agent pi [filter]                # Pi only

126: - Test real agent interactions (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Factory AI Droid, Copilot CLI, Pi, or Vogon creating files, committing, etc.)
